design_detail: National online survey (the Drug Policing Survey, late 2015) with an embedded randomized vignette experiment. 2115 Australians aged 18 or over who had attended an outdoor music festival and a licensed entertainment precinct in the past year, recruited online, were block-randomised to one of four written policing scenarios for a 30,000-person festival: high-visibility policing (over 200 uniformed and plain-clothes police inside and outside); riot policing (over 400 police including public order and riot squads and mounted police); three drug detection ('sniffer') dogs at the gates; or collaborative policing (police working with health organisations, first-aid tents and volunteers). Each participant also answered a no-police scenario (police said to have left before the band they want to see), and after each scenario said whether they would use, possess (carry drugs in), buy inside the grounds, give, or sell illicit drugs. Police presence against no police was compared within person (McNemar tests) and the strategies between blocks (logistic regression). The survey also asked about drug use, supply and police encounters at the last festival attended. The scenarios were built from 114 Australian police media releases and news articles (2002–2014) and focus-group tested. Only the festival half of a ten-scenario survey (the other half concerned licensed entertainment precincts) is reported.
can_establish: That among 2115 young Australian festival-goers recruited online, most of whom had used illicit drugs, stated intentions to use drugs and especially to carry them into a festival were lower in written scenarios with police (most with sniffer dogs) than without, while stated intentions to buy drugs inside the grounds were slightly higher, and that about two-thirds still said they would use drugs under every policing scenario.
cannot_establish: What people actually do when police or sniffer dogs are present (intentions in hypothetical scenarios, not behaviour); whether policing changes how much or which drugs people take, or leads people to swallow drugs to avoid detection (not studied in this paper); or how far the figures describe festival-goers in general (a self-selected online sample with unknown response rate).

sample.recruitment: Online, Australia-wide, mainly through youth, music and drug forums and social media (e.g. Facebook), on drug-specific and other sites (p. 94, Methodology › Sample and recruitment). Of 4117 respondents, 2137 were asked about festivals; 18 were excluded for not consenting or being ineligible (e.g. aged 16) and 4 for invalid responses, leaving 2115.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or older, living in Australia, and attended at least one outdoor music festival and one licensed entertainment precinct in the last year (p. 94).
sample.demographics: Mean age 22.32 (SD 4.65); 54.9% male; 93.0% had completed year 12; 42.4% employed (29.9% full time); 71.3% metropolitan; 40.3% from New South Wales, 26.1% Victoria, 14.3% Queensland. Lifetime illicit drug use 89.1% and recent use 78.4%; cannabis and ecstasy used in the last 12 months by 68.6% and 62.4%. 47.0% had ever been stopped by Australian police, 21.9% searched (e.g. patted down or strip searched), 10.8% ever charged or arrested and 4.9% convicted (pp. 94–95; Table 2).
sample.attrition: The number who started but did not finish the survey is not reported; 22 of 2137 festival respondents were excluded.
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected online sample recruited partly through drug forums, with very high rates of drug use (89% lifetime); no response rate can be computed. The authors report that demographics and drug use were broadly consistent with another national survey of festival-goers and with people who use ecstasy at least monthly (p. 95). Results describe this group, not festival-goers in general.

exposure.measurement: The exposure is the written scenario: the policing strategy described in a short vignette (Table 1, p. 93), randomly assigned between blocks, with every participant also answering the no-police scenario. Actual drug use, supply and police encounters at the last festival were self-reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Participants who said yes were asked which of nine drug categories and what quantity; these answers were collected but not reported in this paper (deferred to later work, p. 99).

comparison.controls: The no-police scenario, answered by every participant (the matched-pairs analysis implies this; the order in which the two scenarios were shown is not reported); in the regressions, the strategies were compared with collaborative policing.
comparison.matching: Randomized blocks were similar on measured characteristics except that the high-visibility block was about one year younger than the collaborative block (mean age 21.89 vs 22.81, p = 0.004) (p. 94; Table 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the within-person comparison; scenario order, attention and seriousness of answers were not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same people answered the control scenario.

outcomes.instruments: Purpose-built online Drug Policing Survey: after each scenario, yes or no to using illicit drugs, possessing them (carrying or taking them into the grounds), buying inside the grounds, giving to a friend or acquaintance inside the grounds (social supply) and selling inside the grounds (for-profit supply); perceived likelihood of detection on a five-point scale; demographic, drug-use, criminal-justice and attitude items drawn from the National Drug Strategy Household Survey, Australian Institute of Criminology, US Bureau of Justice Statistics and EMCDDA instruments; last-festival drug use, supply and police encounters (pp. 93–94). The full instrument is online (p. 94).
outcomes.validity_norms: Scenarios focus-group tested; perceived detection differed between scenarios as intended (a manipulation check); validity of intentions argued from meta-analyses of intention–behaviour correlations (r 0.49–0.79) and from the similarity of stated and last-festival rates (pp. 93, 99). No validation of the survey items is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Deterrence as a lower proportion saying they would commit an offence under a policing scenario than under no police; any offending as any of the five behaviours.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Significance set at 0.001 to adjust for multiple comparisons (p. 94), but results with p = 0.003 to 0.041 are described or marked as significant in the text and tables (see reporting issues). Six offending outcomes were each tested for police against no police and across the four strategies, plus perceived detection and eleven candidate predictors.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-completed online survey); participants knew which scenario they were answering.

analysis.effect_sizes: Proportions saying they would offend (Table 4; any police vs no police): any offence 72.8% vs 77.4% (−4.6 points; McNemar χ²(1) = 61.172, p < 0.001); use 69.6% vs 76.5% (−6.9; χ²(1) = 102.063); possess 52.6% vs 62.8% (−10.2; χ²(1) = 157.228); buy inside 39.5% vs 36.8% (+2.7); give 26.9% vs 28.9% (−2.0); sell 3.5% vs 5.1% (−1.6). By strategy (high-visibility, riot, dogs, collaborative): any offence 70.6, 72.7, 71.2, 76.6% (p = 0.003); use 67.9, 69.2, 66.3, 75.1% (p < 0.001); possess 51.7, 52.0, 47.1, 59.4% (p < 0.001); buy 38.3, 37.9, 43.8, 38.2% (p = 0.711); give 25.0, 26.3, 28.4, 27.9% (p = 0.029); sell 3.0, 3.0, 4.3, 3.6% (p = 0.029). Regression odds ratios against collaborative policing (Table 5): overall offending 2.687 (95% CI 1.495–4.832, high visibility), 2.259 (riot), 2.438 (dogs); possession 2.338, 2.692, 3.170; buying 1.315, 1.312, 1.341 (not significant). Editors' calculation from Table 4: the odds of not offending under high-visibility against collaborative policing are about 1.36, not 2.69, so the regression outcome must differ from the one described (see reporting issues). Absolute differences are a few percentage points.
analysis.covariates: Multivariate model (Table 6): policing strategy, festival frequency, lifetime drug use, age under 24, income, residence, ever encountering police, respect for police, perceived consequences of detection.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or pre-specified analysis plan is reported in the paper.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the festival half of the survey is reported; drug types and quantities were collected but deferred to later work (p. 99), so effects on how much or what people would take are not available.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In written scenarios, any police presence lowered the share saying they would commit any drug offence from 77.4% to 72.8%, mostly through use and carrying drugs in; sniffer dogs lowered stated carrying from 62.8% to 47.1% and stated use from 76.5% to 66.3%, and stated buying inside the grounds rose from 36.8% to 39.5% with any police (43.8% with dogs, though the strategies did not differ significantly on buying). Collaborative policing gave rates close to no police. At their last festival, 65.3% of the sample said they had used illicit drugs, 22.5% had sold or given drugs, and 71.2% had seen police.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says police presence led to a 4.6-point reduction and that buying of drugs increased significantly within festival grounds (p. 91), describing hypothetical intentions as effects; it also says high-visibility policing most reduced overall offending, ‘including supply’ (p. 91), although it differs from drug detection dogs by 0.6 points without a test and the strategies did not differ on supply at the paper's own threshold (giving and selling p = 0.029, buying p = 0.711). The discussion says sniffer dogs lead to the highest rate of buying drugs inside festivals (p. 98), but the strategies did not differ significantly for buying (p = 0.711, Table 4). Statements resting on the regressions (odds 2.3–3.2 times higher than collaborative policing; police presence not the most significant predictor, Fig. 2) depend on models whose outcome is described inconsistently and whose statistics cannot all be reconciled (see reporting issues). The concerns about adulterated drugs bought inside festivals, switching to less detectable drugs, changing quantities or hasty consumption of pills to avoid police come from other sources or are speculation, not data from this survey. The authors state the central limitation, intended rather than actual behaviour (p. 99).

timeline.event: Hughes, Weatherburn and MacCoun (2015): the same team's 2014 pilot with three scenarios in 513 New South Wales festival patrons; police with drug detection dogs led to 9.5% fewer saying they would use illicit drugs than no police (as summarized on p. 92; not read here)
This study: national survey, four policing strategies, use, possession, buying and supply outcomes

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the pilot's finding on drug detection dogs and stated use was repeated here by the same team with the same method; both measure intentions in hypothetical scenarios. No study of actual behaviour is reported in this paper.

funding.funder: Australian Research Council Discovery Project DP150100910; the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre receives funding from the Commonwealth Australian Government; Alison Ritter holds a National Health and Medical Research Council Fellowship (APP1021988) (p. 99, Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that there are no conflicts of interest (p. 99).
funding.affiliations_note: Drug Policy Modelling Program, National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales; New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research; Stanford Law School (p. 91). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study of actual behaviour at festivals with and without drug detection dogs or other policing, for example events or days with policing allocated at random, measuring drug use, carrying, buying inside, amounts taken at once and medical presentations, together with drug checking of what people buy inside the grounds.

domains.note: Block randomization is stated without method or concealment; blocks were similar except for a one-year age difference. For police against no police, each person answered both scenarios in an order that is not reported.
Participants answered the scenario allocated to them; perceived detection differed between scenarios as intended, suggesting the scenarios were read.
Break-offs in the online survey are not reported; 22 of 2137 exclusions are.

The outcome is a stated intention about a hypothetical festival, answered by participants who knew the scenario and had just answered a contrasting one; consistency and social-desirability effects are likely, and no behaviour was measured.

No registration; half the survey reported; quantities and drug types deferred; the stated significance threshold is not applied consistently; the regression outcome is unclear; p values differ between text and table.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The randomized scenario design gives clean comparisons of what this sample said they would do, but the outcome is a hypothetical intention, not behaviour, and the reporting of significance and of the regressions is inconsistent. The paper may be cited for the sizes of the differences in stated intentions in Table 4 (for example carrying drugs in: 62.8% with no police, 47.1% with sniffer dogs; buying inside: 36.8% with no police, 39.5% with any police) and for the last-festival self-reports of this online sample (65.3% used illicit drugs, 22.5% sold or gave drugs, 71.2% saw police). It may not be cited for actual changes in behaviour, for effects on overdoses, drug quantities or swallowing drugs to avoid detection, for the regression odds ratios or predicted probabilities, or as representative of festival-goers.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 2115 people aged 18 or over who had been to an outdoor music festival in the past year, recruited online across Australia (mean age 22.32; 54.9% male); 89.1% had used an illicit drug in their lifetime and 78.4% recently; 47.0% had ever been stopped by Australian police and 21.9% searched.
key_findings.locator: Methodology › Sample and recruitment (p. 94); Results › Demographics and drug use characteristics of the sample (pp. 94–95); Table 2 (p. 94)

key_findings.finding: At the last festival attended: 65.3% of the sample said they had used illicit drugs (ecstasy most often), 22.5% had sold or given drugs to someone (mainly ecstasy), and 71.2% had seen or encountered police; among the types of police seen, drug detection dogs were reported by 43.5%, second to uniformed police (64.0%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug offending and police encounters at the last festival attended, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3
key_findings.note: Table 3's drug-specific rows use an unstated denominator (ecstasy 85.1% is not a share of the whole sample, of whom 65.3% used any drug), and the denominator for types of police seen is not given (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Perceived chance of detection for use or possession was rated likely or very likely by 52.3% under sniffer dogs, 32.9% under riot policing, 26.5% under high-visibility policing, 14.9% under collaborative policing and 1.8% with no police; for supply offences 62.2%, 48%, 41.9%, 26.8% and 3.6%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Perceived likelihood of police detection under different policing vignettes; Fig. 1
key_findings.note: Fig. 1 and this paragraph call the collaborative strategy community policing.

key_findings.finding: Any police presence against no police (stated intentions, Table 4): any drug offence 72.8% vs 77.4% (−4.6 points; McNemar χ²(1) = 61.172, p < 0.001); use 69.6% vs 76.5% (−6.9; χ²(1) = 102.063, p < 0.001); carrying drugs in 62.8% with no police vs 52.6% with police (−10.2; χ²(1) = 157.228, p < 0.001); giving 26.9% vs 28.9% (−2.0) and selling 3.5% vs 5.1% (−1.6); buying inside the grounds rose from 36.8% to 39.5% (+2.7).
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results › Impacts of 'police presence' versus 'no police', both subsections
key_findings.note: The p values for buying, giving and selling differ between the text and Table 4 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: By strategy (Table 4; high-visibility, riot, sniffer dogs, collaborative, no police): would use 67.9, 69.2, 66.3, 75.1 and 76.5%; would carry drugs in 51.7, 52.0, 47.1, 59.4 and 62.8%; would buy inside 38.3, 37.9, 43.8, 38.2 and 36.8%; any offence 70.6, 72.7, 71.2, 76.6 and 77.4%. The p values compare the four strategies only (χ² with 3 degrees of freedom): use and carrying p < 0.001, buying p = 0.711 (no difference), any offence p = 0.003.
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results › Impacts by policing strategy

key_findings.finding: Sniffer dogs produced the largest fall in stated carrying of drugs into the festival, from 62.8% with no police to 47.1% (15.7 points), against 59.4% with collaborative policing (3.4 points); collaborative policing produced no significant reduction in any offence.
key_findings.locator: Results › Impacts by policing strategy › Type of illicit drug offending (p. 96, right column); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 98)

key_findings.finding: Whatever the policing, about two-thirds said they would use illicit drugs and at least 25% said they would engage in some form of supply; the authors compare stated rates under the policing scenarios (use 66.3–69.2%; supply 25.0–28.4%) with those reported for the last festival (65.3% and 22.5%). [Table 4: use under collaborative policing was 75.1%, outside the authors' range, and 25.0–28.4% are the giving rates; no rate for any supply is reported.]
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 98, left column); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 99, left column)

key_findings.finding: People who had ever been stopped by police were less likely to be deterred (adjusted odds ratio 0.587, 95% CI 0.395–0.874); being deterred was more likely with lifetime drug use (3.894), rural residence (2.234), attending festivals only 1–2 times a year (3.403) and perceiving consequences of detection (2.205–2.603).
key_findings.locator: Results › Impacts of policing vis-a-vis other factors, 2nd paragraph (right column); Table 6
key_findings.note: The outcome of these models is described inconsistently and some statistics cannot be reconciled (see reporting issues); cite the direction only.

key_findings.finding: Drug types and quantities were collected but not analysed in this paper (to be examined in later work), so it contains no data on how much people would take, switching to less detectable drugs, or swallowing drugs to avoid police; the hasty-consumption concern in the introduction is attributed to other sources (Hickey et al., 2012, and media and advocacy reports).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, The challenge of policing outdoor music festivals, 3rd paragraph (p. 92); Methodology, 5th paragraph (p. 93); Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 99)

reporting_issues.issue: Significance was set at 0.001 to adjust for multiple comparisons, yet results at p = 0.003 (strategy effect on any offence), 0.005, 0.009, 0.015, 0.017, 0.022 and 0.041 are called or marked significant in the text and Tables 4–6.
reporting_issues.consequence: Under the paper's own threshold, the difference between strategies in overall offending and several predictors in the multivariate model would not be significant.

reporting_issues.issue: The p values for buying, giving and selling differ between text and Table 4: the text gives buying p = 0.001, giving p = 0.001 and selling p = 0.005, Table 4 gives buying < 0.001, giving 0.005 and selling 0.001; the chi-square for giving (11.57, printed with 2115 degrees of freedom) equals that for buying (11.572, 1 degree of freedom).
reporting_issues.consequence: The test results for the supply outcomes cannot be relied on; at least one value appears to have been copied.

reporting_issues.issue: The logistic regressions are described as models of offending (yes or no), but their odds ratios cannot be reproduced from the offending rates in Table 4 (editors' calculation: odds of not offending, high-visibility against collaborative policing, about 1.36 against the printed 2.687); the text calls the outcome being deterred, the multivariate model's 94.0% correct classification fits only a rare outcome such as changing one's answer between scenarios, and the predicted probabilities of deterrence in Fig. 2 (about 0.5 to 0.77) fit neither reading.
reporting_issues.consequence: The regression odds ratios and Fig. 2 should not be cited for magnitudes; the percentages in Table 4 are the interpretable result.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 and the text disagree on drug use at the last festival: the text says ecstasy was reported by 85.1% of the sample, although only 65.3% of the sample used any drug; hallucinogens are 10.2% in the text and 20.8% in Table 3; ecstasy supply (22.9%) exceeds any supply (22.5%). Denominators of the drug-specific rows are not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Drug-specific last-festival percentages cannot be cited as shares of the sample.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 53.2% attended a festival 1–2 times in the past year; Table 2 gives 58.4% overall, which matches its block values (editors' check).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table value is internally consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: Typographical errors in Tables 5–6: a p printed as 0.35 for an odds ratio of 3.500 whose interval (1.093–11.209) excludes 1 (editors' calculation about 0.035); the giving comparison for dogs against collaborative policing printed as p = 0.035 although its interval (1.269–3.725) implies about 0.005; an upper limit printed as 3982; some intervals asymmetric around their estimates on the log scale.
reporting_issues.consequence: Individual regression statistics are unreliable; this adds to the concerns about the models.

reporting_issues.issue: The order of the two scenarios each person answered is not reported, and the no-police scenario differs from the others in more than policing (police said to have left before a late-afternoon band); the scenarios also differ in information source (friend, social media post, organisers' notice, hearsay) and, for collaborative policing, in the health services offered.
reporting_issues.consequence: Order and wording effects cannot be separated from the effect of policing on stated intentions.
